words.gloss: those things which do not last (accusative)

ai.literal: Those things which do not stand, as permanent things, thus believing, that possession of low wisdom, is the lowest state.
ai.translation: To mistake transient things for permanent realities is the lowest form of ignorance.
ai.modern: நிலைத்து நிற்காத பொருள்களை நிலையானவை என்று நம்புகின்ற சிற்றறிவுடைமை மிக இழிவானதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the lowest level of ignorance, termed 'pullarivanmai' (poor understanding). It occurs when a person mistakes transient, fleeting things (nillathavatrai) for eternal, permanent realities (nilaiyina). The author calls this delusion the lowest state (kadai) of human intellect. Recognizing the impermanent nature of worldly things is the first step toward true wisdom.

ai.literal: Like the gathering of a crowd for a dance performance is great wealth; its departure is like that crowd dispersing.
ai.translation: The gathering of great wealth is like a crowd assembling to watch a play; its departure is like that same crowd dispersing when the show is over.
ai.modern: பெரிய செல்வம் சேருவது கூத்து நடக்கும் இடத்திற்கு மக்கள் கூட்டம் கூடுவது போன்றது; அச்செல்வம் அழிந்து போவது அக்கூட்டம் கலைந்து போவது போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid theatrical metaphor to explain the impermanence of wealth. The gathering of great wealth is compared to a crowd assembling to watch a dance performance—it happens gradually and looks grand. However, just as the crowd quickly disperses and vanishes once the show is over, the accumulated wealth can disappear in an instant. The key words 'கூத்தாட்டு அவை' (dance drama assembly) and 'விளிந்து' (disappearing/dispersing) highlight how transient worldly possessions are, urging us not to cling to them.

ai.literal: Impermanent is the nature of wealth; if that is obtained, things that endure, immediately, should be done.
ai.translation: Wealth is of an impermanent nature; if you obtain it, immediately perform those deeds that are of a lasting nature.
ai.modern: செல்வம் நிலைவில்லாத தன்மையுடையது; அதனைப் பெற்றால், அப்பொழுதே நிலைத்து நிற்கும் அறச்செயல்களைச் செய்ய வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the fleeting nature of material wealth and advises on its immediate, wise utilization. The word 'அற்கா' means impermanent or non-abiding, describing the true nature ('இயல்பிற்று') of wealth ('செல்வம்'). Since wealth can vanish at any moment, the author urges that if one happens to acquire it ('அதுபெற்றால்'), they must immediately ('ஆங்கே') use it to perform deeds that have a lasting value ('அற்குப செயல்'), such as acts of virtue and charity. By converting transient wealth into enduring good deeds, one achieves something of permanent value before the opportunity slips away.

ai.literal: A day, showing itself like a mere unit of time, is actually a saw that cuts away life, if there are those who understand it.
ai.translation: To those who have the wisdom to understand, a day is a saw that, while appearing to be just a measure of time, continuously cuts away at their life.
ai.modern: நாள் என்று சொல்லப்படும் ஒரு எளிய கால அளவு போலத் தன்னைக் காட்டி, உயிரை அறுத்துக் கொண்டிருக்கும் வாள் ஆகும் அது, அதனை ஆராய்ந்து உணர்வாரைப் பெற்றால்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a powerful metaphor to illustrate the impermanence of life. To an ordinary person, a day seems like a harmless unit of time passing by. However, to those who possess deep understanding, each passing day is actually a saw ('வாள்') that is steadily cutting away ('ஈரும்') at their lifespan ('உயிர்'). The word 'ஈரும்' specifically refers to the action of sawing or slicing, emphasizing the gradual but relentless reduction of our remaining time on earth.

ai.literal: Before the hiccup comes upwards blocking the tongue, good deeds must be eagerly gone and done.
ai.translation: Before the final hiccup rises up and blocks the tongue, one must hasten to perform good deeds.
ai.modern: நாக்கை அடைத்துக்கொண்டு விக்கல் மேலே எழுந்து வருவதற்கு முன்பாகவே, நற்செயல்களை விரைந்து சென்று செய்ய வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the extreme transience of human life and urges immediate action. The poet uses the striking physical image of a dying person's last hiccup rising and blocking the tongue to represent the suddenness of death. Since we cannot predict when this final moment will silence us, we must not delay our moral duties. Instead, we should actively go forward and perform virtuous deeds while we still have the breath of life.

ai.literal: Yesterday he was present, one person; today he is not, saying [this] greatness possesses this world.
ai.translation: This world possesses the mighty reputation that a person who was alive yesterday is no more today.
ai.modern: நேற்று இருந்த ஒருவன் இன்று இல்லை என்று சொல்லும் பெருமையை இந்த உலகம் பெற்றுள்ளது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute transience of human life. The word 'perumai' (greatness or distinction) is used here with solemn irony to describe the world's defining power of impermanence. By contrasting 'nerunal' (yesterday) with 'iṉṟu' (today), the poet shows how quickly life can vanish. The greatness of this world lies in its constant reminder that no one, no matter how powerful, is guaranteed another day.

ai.literal: Even for a single moment, their living, they do not know; (yet) they think of ten million and more other many things.
ai.translation: Those who do not even know if they will live for another moment plan for ten million things and more.
ai.modern: ஒரு நிமிடம் கூடத் தாங்கள் உயிர் வாழ்வதை உறுதி செய்யத் தெரியாதவர்கள், கோடிக்கும் மேலான பல எண்ணங்களை எண்ணித் திட்டமிடுகிறார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the profound ignorance of human beings regarding the impermanence of life. The poet points out that people cannot guarantee their own survival even for a single moment (orupozhutu). Yet, despite this extreme uncertainty, their minds are constantly occupied with planning and desiring millions of things (kotiyum alla pala) for the future. The contrast between the fragility of a single moment of life and the vastness of human desires emphasizes the theme of impermanence.

ai.literal: The nest alone to be left behind, a bird having flown, is just like that, the friendship between the body and the life.
ai.translation: The relationship between the body and the soul is just like a bird that flies away, leaving its empty nest behind.
ai.modern: கூடு தனியாகக் கைவிடப்பட்டு ஒழிய, பறவை பறந்து போவதைப் போன்றதே உடம்பிற்கும் உயிருக்கும் இடையே உள்ள நட்பு ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the impermanence of life using a vivid natural metaphor. The poet compares the human body to a nest and the soul to a bird. Just as a bird resides in a nest temporarily and flies away, leaving the nest completely empty and abandoned, the soul dwells in the body only for a short time before departing. The word 'natpu' (friendship) is used here to describe the connection between body and soul, highlighting that even this intimate bond is temporary and destined to end abruptly.

ai.literal: Sleeping is like death; having slept, waking up is like birth.
ai.translation: Death is like falling asleep, and birth is like waking up after sleep.
ai.modern: இறப்பு என்பது உறங்குவதைப் போன்றது; உறங்கிவிட்டு விழித்தெழுவது போன்றது பிறப்பு.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the concept of impermanence and the cycle of life using a simple, everyday analogy. Death is compared to falling asleep, which is a natural, temporary state of rest. Birth is compared to waking up after that sleep. By equating these grand cosmic transitions to the familiar daily cycle of sleeping and waking, the poet demystifies death and shows that life is a continuous journey of transitions.

ai.literal: A permanent home is not established indeed, for the soul that resided in a temporary lodging within the body.
ai.translation: Has a permanent home not been established for the soul, that it has to reside in this temporary lodging of a body?
ai.modern: உடம்பாகிய தற்காலிகக் குடிலில் தங்கியிருந்த உயிர்க்கு, நிலையானதொரு புகலிடம் இன்னும் அமையவில்லை போலும்!
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the temporary nature of the physical body with the journey of the soul. The poet uses two key words: 'tuccil', which refers to a makeshift, temporary shelter or hut, and 'pukkil', which means a secure, permanent home. The body is described as a mere temporary lodging where the soul stays briefly. The poet wonders with a sense of irony ('kollō') whether the soul is forced to live in such a fragile, temporary body only because it has not yet found its true, permanent resting place.
